title: Is SEO Dead With AI? What Actually Changes in 2026
metaTitle: Is SEO Dead With AI in 2026?
metaDescription: Is SEO dead with AI? No. AI Overviews changed how people search, but crawlability, structured data, and genuine expertise still decide who ranks today.
excerpt: Is SEO dead with AI? No, but the tactics that earn visibility changed. Here's the direct answer: what AI Overviews changed, what to drop, and what still ranks in 2026.
author: Prabal Raj Shakya
body:
Key Takeaways

  • SEO is not dead in 2026. AI changed which tactics rank a page, not whether ranking matters.
  • AI Overviews summarize crawled, well-structured, already-ranking pages. A page that couldn't rank before still won't get cited now.
  • Traditional SEO tactics like keyword stuffing and link schemes stopped working years ago. Crawlability, site speed, and structured data optimization matter more than ever.
  • Optimizing for LLMs and SEO overlap almost completely: both systems reward relevance, clarity, and real expertise.
  • Content marketing isn't dead either. AI systems replace generic, templated content, not substantive work written by someone who actually knows the subject.
  • SEO remains a strong career in 2026, now built around technical skills and AI-search literacy instead of link-building tricks.

Is SEO dead with AI? No. SEO isn't dead in 2026, but AI has rewritten which tactics earn visibility and which ones waste your time. I run SEO audits for a living, and every audit I run now checks the same thing a person checks and the same thing an AI system checks: can this page be crawled, does it answer the question directly, and does a real expert stand behind it. That test hasn't changed. What's changed is who's reading the page.

Why "Is SEO Dead" Keeps Coming Back

This question resurfaces every time search changes shape, and the history of SEO backs that up. Mobile-first indexing triggered it. Voice search triggered it. Now generative AI triggers it. Each cycle produces the same panic and the same wave of "SEO is dead" articles, and each cycle ends the same way: the fundamentals survive because search engines still crawl a page, still parse what it means, and still decide whether it deserves a spot in front of someone searching. AI didn't remove that process. It added a second audience reading the same output.

What AI Overviews Actually Changed in Search

Organic search still runs the show. What changed is the first thing a searcher sees. Google's AI Overviews now open a growing share of informational SERPs with a generated summary before any ranked link appears, and some searchers stop there and never click through.

That shift matters most for simple, single-answer questions. It matters far less for commercial, comparison, and decision-heavy searches, where people still read full pages, compare real options, and check who wrote the content before they hire someone or buy something.

Does This Mean AI Overviews Are Surely Going to Kill SEO?

No. AI Overviews don't invent answers from nothing. They summarize crawled, indexed, well-structured pages that already rank through the exact mechanisms behind normal organic search. A thin, unstructured, hard-to-crawl page wasn't ranking before AI Overviews existed, and generative AI didn't change that outcome.

Getting cited inside an AI Overview is a real visibility win, similar to how featured snippets worked before it. And plenty of queries, especially local and transactional searches, still send people straight into a normal set of ranked results. AI Overviews reshaped the SERP. They didn't erase the competition to rank well within it.

"SEO Is Outdated," Separating the Myth From the Reality

This claim is half right. Specific SEO tactics are outdated. SEO as a discipline is not, and confusing the two costs businesses real traffic.

Traditional SEO Tactics That No Longer Work

  • Keyword stuffing: cramming a phrase into a sentence instead of writing for a real reader
  • Exact-match anchor text link schemes and paid link farms
  • Publishing thin, templated pages for every keyword variation instead of consolidating one strong page
  • Chasing seo algorithm loopholes instead of building something genuinely useful
  • Ignoring page experience: slow load times, intrusive pop-ups, broken mobile layouts

Drop any of these traditional SEO tactics today and you lose nothing, because Google's ranking systems already discount them.

SEO Isn't Dead, It's Redistributed

Crawlability, site speed, and structured data optimization matter more now, not less, because both traditional ranking systems and AI retrieval systems depend on the exact same technical baseline: a crawler has to reach the page, read it cleanly, and understand what it covers before either system can use it. SEO's core job, making a site easy to find, easy to understand, and worth ranking, never left. It just stopped being optional for AI systems reading the same pages.

How to Optimize for LLMs and SEO Together

Optimizing for LLMs and SEO overlaps more than most people expect, because both systems chase the same three signals: relevance, clarity, and trust.

Five moves cover both at once:

  1. Add structured data (schema markup) so machines can parse what a page covers and who wrote it
  2. Put a direct, specific answer near the top of the page instead of three paragraphs of preamble
  3. Show real expertise and authorship (E-E-A-T), since search algorithms and AI systems both weigh who's behind the content
  4. Build a logical heading structure (H1, H2, H3) that mirrors how a person actually asks the question
  5. Fix technical delivery speed, because a slow or broken page loses ranking with crawlers and gets skipped by AI retrieval systems too

The seo algorithm behind classic rankings and the retrieval systems behind AI Overviews reward the same signals through different interfaces, not different signals entirely.

The SEO Process Hasn't Disappeared, It's Sharper

What "Crawling" Actually Means in SEO

Crawling meaning in SEO, stated plainly: an automated program, an SEO crawler like Googlebot, follows links from page to page and downloads what it finds. The index stores that content, and ranking systems measure it against relevance and trust signals whenever someone searches. AI systems largely reuse this same crawling infrastructure, or run their own crawler built the same way, to source what they cite. A crawler that can't reach your page can't rank it, and an AI system can't cite it either.

Running a New SEO Campaign in 2026

A new SEO campaign still follows a recognizable process; it just carries a sharper technical layer now:

  1. Run a real SEO audit report covering crawlability, site speed, and structured data, not just a keyword list
  2. Pull real search demand from a seo keyword generator or research tool, and match content to actual intent instead of guesses
  3. Fix the technical baseline first: crawlability, page speed, mobile usability, structured data
  4. Build content around real questions, organized so both people and AI systems can follow the structure
  5. Track rankings, AI Overview citations where you can see them, and actual traffic and conversions, not just position

Is Content Marketing Dead?

No. Content marketing matters more now, because AI systems need substantive, well-organized content to summarize and cite in the first place. What's dying is generic, keyword-stuffed content built to rank instead of to answer something real. A specific, well-researched article from someone who actually works the subject is harder for AI systems to replace, not easier, because that expert work is the exact source material those systems draw from. None of this changes the importance of SEO for a business that still needs real customers to find it.

Is SEO a Good Career in 2026?

Yes, and it's a more interesting career than it was five years ago. The skill set broadened: technical SEO, structured data, content strategy, and a working grasp of how AI retrieval systems source information now sit inside the job description, not outside it. Businesses still need someone who can make a site fast, crawlable, well-structured, and genuinely useful, and that demand didn't shrink just because the SERP looks different.

SEO Isn't Dead, It's a Different Game

Organic search still runs, SERPs still exist, the seo algorithm still ranks pages, and AI Overviews still pull their answers from crawled, well-structured content. What changed is which tactics earn that visibility. Keyword stuffing and link schemes are finished. Crawlability, site speed, structured data optimization, real expertise, and content built to answer an actual question are what's left, and they carry more weight now, not less.

Quick Answers (FAQ)

Is SEO dead in 2026?

No. AI changed the ranking inputs, not the outcome businesses need: visibility in organic search and inside AI Overviews.

Is SEO outdated?

Specific traditional SEO tactics are outdated. SEO optimization built around crawlability, structured data, and real expertise is not.

Is content marketing dead?

No. Generic content is what AI systems replace. Expert, specific content is what they cite.

Is SEO a good career in 2026?

Yes. The role now demands technical SEO skills and AI-search literacy, which raises its value rather than lowering it.

Where This Leaves Your Website

Run a real audit before you touch anything else. A proper technical and content review shows exactly where a site loses visibility, whether that's crawlability gaps, missing structured data, outdated pages, or a mismatch against what people search for now.

PS

About the Author

Written by Prabal Raj Shakya, an SEO freelancer in Nepal who runs technical and content audits for client sites and tracks these exact changes in live campaigns.

title: What Is the 3-3-3 Rule in Marketing?
metaTitle: What Is the 3-3-3 Rule in Marketing? Full Guide
metaDescription: The 3-3-3 rule in marketing uses three content types, three distribution channels, and three buyer journey stages to build a simple growth framework.
excerpt: The 3-3-3 rule in marketing uses three content types, three distribution channels, and three buyer journey stages to build a simple growth framework.
author: Prabal Raj Shakya
body:
If you've been searching for a simple way to structure your content strategy, the 3-3-3 rule in marketing is a good place to start. It breaks your strategy into three content types, three distribution channels, and three stages of the buyer's journey, so every piece of content has a clear job to do. Some marketers call it the rule of 3 in marketing or marketing rule of three, but the idea stays the same: three inputs, three channels, three moments in the customer's decision. Below is a 3-3-3 rule in marketing example you can apply to your own brand.

Key Takeaways

• The 3-3-3 rule in marketing organizes your strategy around three content types, three distribution channels, and three buyer journey stages.

• It works as a simple marketing framework for small business teams that don't have time for complicated content plans.

• Mapping content to awareness, consideration, decision helps you avoid publishing content nobody needs yet.

• Distribution matters as much as creation, so picking the right key distribution channels in marketing determines whether content gets seen.

• A basic buyer persona helps you decide which three content types and channels actually fit your audience.


The 3 Pillars Of The 3-3-3 Rule Of Marketing

Every version of this approach rests on three pillars: content, distribution, and the buyer's journey. Together they form a content marketing framework for brand growth that's easy to remember, because it forces you to think about who you're creating for, how you're reaching them, and when they actually want it.

Three Content Types to Engage Your Audience

The first pillar covers content types to engage your audience at different points in their decision-making. Rather than producing one format over and over, choose three that work together, for example a blog post for search visibility, a short video for social engagement, and a case study for proof. Rotating between three content types keeps things varied without overwhelming your team.

Three Key Distribution Channels

The second pillar is about picking key distribution channels in marketing and sticking to them. Trying to be everywhere at once usually means being mediocre everywhere. A focused content distribution strategy might rely on organic search, email, and one social platform where your audience actually spends time. When you understand marketing distribution channels explained in the context of your specific audience, three channels done well will always outperform ten done poorly.

Three Stages Of Buyer Journey

The third pillar maps content to the three stages of the buyer's journey. This is the connective tissue of the whole framework. Buyer journey stages explained simply: awareness is when someone realizes they have a problem, consideration is when they compare solutions, and decision is when they choose a provider. This awareness, consideration, decision path is what customer journey mapping is really tracking, and it's how you learn how to align content with buyer journey expectations instead of guessing.

How To Use the 3-3-3 Rule Of Marketing For Brand Growth

Start with a buyer persona. Before choosing content types or channels, get clear on who you're writing for and what they care about at each stage. From there, apply the framework to your own business:

• Pick three content types: blog articles, short-form video, and case studies.

• Pick three distribution channels: organic search, email newsletter, and one core social platform.

• Map each content type to a buyer journey stage: awareness content answers broad questions, consideration content compares options, decision content builds trust.

 

This structure works well for a small business owner because it limits your choices. You're not trying to master every platform or format, you're building a repeatable system: three inputs, three outputs, three moments in the customer's decision. Review your content marketing plan quarterly, and swap a channel or content type only if the data shows it isn't pulling weight.

Used consistently, this rule becomes an operating rhythm for your brand growth strategy: create with intention, distribute with focus, and meet the buyer wherever they are in the journey.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the 3-3-3 rule in marketing?

The 3-3-3 rule in marketing is a simple framework that organizes your content strategy around three content types, three distribution channels, and three stages of the buyer's journey. It helps teams create and distribute content with a clear purpose instead of producing content at random.

What are the three pillars of the 3-3-3 rule of marketing?

The three pillars are content types, distribution channels, and buyer journey stages. Each pillar asks a different question: what will you create, where will you share it, and who is it for at each point in their decision.

Is the 3-3-3 rule the same as the rule of three in marketing?

They're closely related. The rule of three in marketing is the broader principle that grouping ideas, channels, or messages in threes makes them easier to remember and act on. The 3-3-3 rule in marketing applies that same principle specifically to content, distribution, and the buyer's journey.

What's an example of the 3-3-3 rule in marketing?

A small business might choose blog posts, short-form video, and case studies as its three content types; organic search, email, and one social platform as its three distribution channels; and awareness, consideration, and decision as its three buyer journey stages, then map each content type to the stage it serves best.

How do I choose the right three distribution channels?

Start with where your buyer persona already spends time, not where it's trendy to post. A focused content distribution strategy across two or three channels you can maintain consistently will outperform a thin presence spread across many.

Does the 3-3-3 rule work for small businesses?

Yes. It works well as a simple marketing framework for small business teams specifically because it limits scope: three content types and three channels are enough to stay consistent without needing a large team or budget.

title: On-Page SEO: What to Fix on a Page Before You Chase Links
metaDescription: On-page SEO explained with a clear checklist: titles, headings, content, internal links and images, plus how it differs from off-page and technical SEO.
excerpt: On-page SEO explained with a clear checklist: titles, headings, content, internal links and images, plus how it differs from off-page and technical SEO.
coverAlt: Cover: on-page SEO guide with a web page wireframe
author: Prabal Raj Shakya
body:
Key Takeaways

  • Start with intent. A page ranks when it gives the searcher what they came for. Keywords come second.
  • Seven elements do most of the work: title tag, URL, headings, opening answer, body content, internal links and images.
  • On-page is the cheapest SEO win. You control it fully, so fix it before spending on links.
  • Titles earn clicks; content earns the ranking. A good title on a thin page still fails.
  • Measure by query, not by page. Check which searches a page appears for, then edit toward the ones that matter.
From my own work: At GSA Contract Services I optimise meta titles and descriptions in RankMath, because accurate on-page metadata affects both rankings and the click-through rate from the results page. The steps below follow how I approach on-page work there.

On-page SEO is everything you control directly on a page that helps search engines and readers understand what it is about and whether it deserves to rank: the title, headings, content, internal links, images and the way the page answers the query it targets. It is the part of SEO you can fix this week without anyone else’s permission.

This guide shows what to change, in what order, how on-page SEO differs from off-page and technical SEO, and how to tell whether your edits worked.

New to SEO? Start with what SEO is and how it works, then come back here.

What on-page SEO covers, and what it does not

The three main branches of SEO answer three different questions. On-page asks, "Does this page deserve to rank for this search?"

On-page SEOOff-page SEOTechnical SEO
Question it answersIs this page the best answer?Do others trust this site?Can a search engine reach and read it?
Where the work happensOn the page itselfAway from your siteIn the site’s code and setup
Typical tasksTitles, headings, copy, internal links, image alt textBacklinks, mentions, reviews, PRCrawling, indexing, speed, redirects, schema
Who controls itYou, fullyPartly, you earn itYou and your developer
How fast it showsOften weeks after re-crawlSlow, compoundingFast once a blocker is removed
Main riskWriting for the keyword, not the personBuying links that backfireBreaking indexing by accident

On-page vs off-page vs technical SEO: how they differ in practice

On-page vs off-page

On-page tells a search engine what a page is about. Off-page tells it that other people agree the page is worth reading, mainly through links from other sites. A page with great content and no links can struggle in competitive searches. A page with many links and weak content tends to slip when a better answer appears. You need both, but on-page is where to begin because it costs only time.

On-page vs technical

Technical SEO decides whether a page can be found and processed at all. On-page SEO decides how well it competes once it is. If a page is blocked or not indexed, polishing its headings does nothing. If it is indexed and fast but vague, technical fixes will not make it rank.

On-page for people vs for search engines

The two goals point the same way more often than not. A clear title, a direct answer, scannable headings and helpful images serve readers and give search engines cleaner signals. The mistakes come when the page is written for the keyword: repeated phrases, padded intros, and headings that read like search queries glued together.

Where on-page SEO fits in your SEO plan

Think of SEO as a sequence. First make sure the site can be crawled and indexed (technical). Then make each important page the best answer to its query (on-page). Then earn the trust that lifts those pages above competitors (off-page).

If your {{link:technical-seo|technical SEO basics}} are broken, fix those first. Once pages are indexed, on-page changes are usually the fastest way to move rankings, and they support everything that follows, including {{link:off-page-seo|off-page SEO}}.

What to fix first: a decision guide

Start from what you see in Google Search Console, not from a generic checklist.

What you seeDo firstWhy
Page not indexedTechnical fix, then on-pageOn-page edits cannot help a page Google has not stored.
Impressions but few clicksRewrite title and meta descriptionYou are showing up but not winning the click.
Position 8 to 20 for a target queryStrengthen content, headings, internal linksYou are close. Better coverage of the topic can lift you to page one.
Ranking for the wrong queriesRe-align the page to its intentThe page answers a different question from the one you want.
Rankings were fine and then droppedCompare against pages now ranking aboveA competitor may now answer the query more completely.

How to do on-page SEO, step by step

Work through one important page at a time, in this order.

  1. Define the one query and intent. Search it yourself. Note what the top results are: guides, product pages, lists, videos. Match that format.
  2. Write the title tag for the click. Put the main phrase near the front, make it specific, and keep it short enough to display. One page, one promise.
  3. Write the meta description as a pitch. It is not a direct ranking factor, but a clear one improves the chance someone clicks.
  4. Use one H1 and logical H2s and H3s. Headings should tell the story of the page when read on their own. Use natural wording that covers the subtopics people expect.
  5. Answer the query early. Give the answer in the first paragraph, then add depth, examples and evidence. First-hand experience is what generic pages lack.
  6. Clean up the URL. Short, readable, lowercase, with words rather than IDs. Avoid changing a URL that already ranks unless you add a redirect.
  7. Add internal links with descriptive anchors. Link from related pages into this one, and from this page to related pages. "Our guide to local SEO" tells more than "click here".
  8. Optimise images. Compress, use modern formats, give each a descriptive file name and honest alt text, and set width and height so the page does not jump.
  9. Add structured data where it matches the page, such as Article, Product or FAQ, but only for content that is visible.
  10. Show who wrote it and when it was updated. This supports trust, especially on topics where accuracy matters.

Before and after: a title tag and opening.

BeforeAfter
Title: "Home | Services | Welcome to Our Digital Agency"
Opening: "We are a leading company providing a wide range of solutions."		Title: "SEO Services in Kathmandu: Audits, Content and Reporting"
Opening: "We help Kathmandu businesses get found on Google with technical audits, content and monthly reporting. Most projects start with a two-week audit."

The second version names the service, the place and what the client gets. Replace the details with your own real offer.

Want a page-by-page on-page SEO review?

Send me your most important pages and I'll check titles, headings, content and internal links against this checklist.

Request an on-page reviewSee my SEO expertise

On-page checklist you can print

  • One clear target query and intent for the page.
  • Title tag: specific, front-loaded, not truncated, unique.
  • Meta description: written for people, unique.
  • One H1; H2s and H3s that cover the subtopics.
  • Answer within the first screen of text.
  • Original examples, data or experience, not a rewrite of the top results.
  • Internal links in and out with descriptive anchors.
  • Images compressed, described and sized.
  • Mobile layout readable with no sideways scrolling.
  • Author, date and sources visible.

A 30-day on-page plan

WeekFocusOutput
1Pick pagesList your 10 most valuable pages. Pull queries, impressions, clicks and position from Search Console.
2Titles and intentRewrite titles and meta descriptions. Re-check each page’s intent against what ranks.
3Content and structureImprove headings, add missing subtopics, add first-hand examples, tighten intros.
4Links, images, reviewAdd internal links, fix images, then record a baseline for comparison next month.

How to measure whether on-page changes worked

Compare like with like, and give Google time to re-crawl.

  1. Record a baseline for each edited page: clicks, impressions, average position and click-through rate for its main queries.
  2. Annotate the date you changed it.
  3. Check after four to eight weeks. Smaller changes can show sooner, but a fair test needs time.
  4. Look at queries, not only the page. A page may gain new queries even if its main one is flat.
  5. Watch engagement: scroll depth, time on page and conversions tell you if the right people are landing.
MetricSourceTells you
Click-through rateSearch ConsoleWhether title and description work
Average position by querySearch ConsoleWhether content changes helped
Impressions growthSearch ConsoleWhether the page matches more queries
Engagement and conversionsAnalyticsWhether visitors found what they wanted

Seven on-page mistakes to avoid

  1. Stuffing the keyword. If it reads oddly aloud, it is too much.
  2. One title for many pages. Each page needs its own promise.
  3. Ignoring intent. A sales page will not rank for a "how to" query.
  4. Thin pages. Short pages with nothing original give search engines no reason to choose you.
  5. Orphan pages. Pages with no internal links are hard to find and easy to ignore.
  6. Missing alt text or oversized images. They hurt accessibility and speed.
  7. Changing everything at once. You will not know what worked.

Frequently asked questions

What is on-page SEO in simple words?

It is improving the things on a page itself, such as the title, headings, content, links and images, so search engines and readers can tell what it is about and that it answers the question well.

Is the meta description a ranking factor?

It is not a direct ranking factor, but a good one can raise the number of people who click your result, which helps in practice.

How many times should I use the keyword?

There is no ideal number. Use the main phrase where it reads naturally, cover related terms, and focus on answering the query completely.

How long does on-page SEO take to work?

You may see changes within a few weeks once the page is re-crawled. Competitive queries often take longer.

Is on-page SEO enough on its own?

Not always. It is necessary, but competitive searches also need trust signals from outside your site, covered by off-page SEO, and a technically sound site.

Conclusion

On-page SEO is the foundation you fully control. Choose a page, define the intent, write a title that earns the click, answer the question early and build depth with real examples. Then connect it to the rest of your site with clear internal links.

If you want an expert review of where your pages stand, get in touch and I will go through your top ten pages against this checklist.

Ready to put this into practice?

Tell me about your site and your goals. I will reply within a day with where I would start.

Get in touchSee my SEO expertise

title: Off-Page SEO Explained: What Builds Authority Beyond Your Website
metaDescription: Off-page SEO explained: how backlinks, brand mentions, reviews and digital PR build trust, how it differs from on-page SEO, and a safe plan to start.
excerpt: Off-page SEO explained: how backlinks, brand mentions, reviews and digital PR build trust, how it differs from on-page SEO, and a safe plan to start.
coverAlt: Cover: off-page SEO guide with a network of linked nodes
author: Prabal Raj Shakya
body:
Key Takeaways

  • Links are votes, but not all votes count equally. A relevant link from a trusted site outweighs many weak ones.
  • Mentions matter too. Unlinked brand mentions and reviews shape how you are seen by people and by AI tools.
  • Earn, do not buy. Paid or manipulative links can bring penalties. Create something worth linking to.
  • Relevance beats volume. Ten links from sites your customers read are worth more than a hundred from unrelated ones.
  • Off-page is slow and compounding. Plan in quarters, not weeks.
From my own work: I run SEO for a company website and track organic performance in Search Console and Analytics, so I treat links as one signal among several, not a goal in themselves. I have written this guide around what Google's own spam policies allow.

Off-page SEO is everything that happens away from your own site that helps search engines trust it, mainly backlinks from other websites acting as votes of confidence. It also includes brand mentions, reviews, and the way other people talk about you across the web.

This guide explains what counts, what does not, how off-page differs from on-page SEO, how to earn links without breaking the rules, and how to measure progress.

New to SEO? Start with what SEO is and how it works, then come back here.

What counts as off-page SEO

Off-page SEO is the trust side of search. It asks, "Do other credible sources point to this site and speak well of it?"

SignalWhat it isWhy it matters
BacklinksLinks from other sites to yoursThe classic vote of confidence
Brand mentionsYour name cited without a linkBuilds recognition and context
Reviews and ratingsCustomer feedback on third-party platformsBuilds trust, strongly for local and ecommerce
Digital PRCoverage earned through news-worthy workBrings high-quality links and mentions
Social and communityDiscussion in forums and social platformsSpreads content and builds awareness
Directory and profile listingsAccurate business listingsConsistent facts and local visibility

Social shares and likes are not a confirmed direct ranking factor, but the attention they create often leads to links and mentions.

Off-page vs on-page vs technical SEO

Off-page vs on-page

On-page work tells search engines what a page is about. Off-page work shows that others value it. A well-written page with no external support may struggle in competitive searches, while a heavily linked page with poor content is vulnerable when someone publishes a better answer.

Backlinks vs brand mentions

A backlink passes a measurable signal. A mention builds recognition, and increasingly it feeds how AI tools describe you. Both come from the same activity: being useful enough that others talk about you.

Earned, editorial links vs manufactured links

Earned links come from people choosing to reference your work. Manufactured links are placed to influence rankings, such as paid links without the right attributes or networks built for the purpose. Google’s spam policies treat link schemes as a violation, so the short-term gain risks a long-term loss.

Where off-page SEO fits in your plan

Off-page comes after the site can be found and the key pages are strong. Building links to a page that is slow, thin or not indexed wastes effort. Fix {{link:technical-seo|technical SEO}} and {{link:on-page-seo|on-page SEO}} first, then amplify the best pages.

For local businesses, off-page also means consistent listings and reviews. See {{link:local-seo|local SEO}}.

Which off-page tactic should you start with?

Choose by the resources you have, not by what looks impressive.

Your situationStart withWhy
New site, small budgetProfiles and listings, then helpful content others citeLow cost, builds a base of consistent facts.
Local businessGoogle Business Profile reviews, local directoriesReviews and consistent details drive local trust.
B2B or expert serviceOriginal data, guest expertise, podcastsAuthority is earned through demonstrated knowledge.
EcommerceReviews, product placements, comparison coverageShoppers rely on third-party proof.
Established site with good contentDigital PR and link reclamationPromote what is already strong.

How to build off-page SEO safely

Use methods that survive a policy update.

  1. Create a linkable asset. Original data, a free tool, a clear guide, a template or an expert opinion that others will cite.
  2. Find who already covers the topic. Journalists, bloggers, newsletters and communities in your field.
  3. Pitch with value. Explain why their audience would care, in two or three sentences, with a link to the asset. No mass templates.
  4. Reclaim lost links and mentions. Search for your brand name and fix broken or unlinked mentions by asking politely.
  5. Be a source. Share expert comments on topics you know, in reputable outlets and communities.
  6. Build reviews the honest way. Ask real customers and respond to all feedback.
  7. Keep listings consistent. Same name, address, phone and description everywhere.
  8. Use the right link attributes. Mark sponsored or paid placements as sponsored, and user-generated links appropriately.

A pitch that gets read, and one that does not.

WeakBetter
"Hi, I love your blog. Please add a link to my website.""Hi [Name], your piece on [topic] listed three options. We tested a fourth with [real result]. Here is the short write-up if it is useful for your readers."

The better version offers something new and specific. Use a real result of your own.

Not sure which links help and which hurt?

I'll review your link profile, brand mentions and reviews, then suggest a safe plan.

Request a link profile reviewSee my SEO expertise

Healthy link profile checklist

  • Links come from sites related to your topic or audience.
  • Anchor text looks natural and varied, mostly brand and descriptive.
  • No sudden bursts of low-quality links.
  • Paid placements carry the sponsored attribute.
  • Your brand mentions are accurate and consistent.
  • Reviews are recent and answered.
  • Broken backlinks are redirected to a relevant live page.

A 90-day off-page plan

WeeksFocusOutput
1 to 2AuditReview current links, mentions, reviews and listings. Note gaps and risky links.
3 to 6FoundationsFix listings, claim profiles, start the review routine, reclaim unlinked mentions.
7 to 10Linkable assetPublish one original asset. List 30 relevant targets.
11 to 13Outreach and reviewSend personalised pitches. Track coverage, links and referral traffic. Decide what to repeat.

How to measure off-page SEO

Count quality and outcomes, not just totals.

  1. Record a baseline of referring domains, brand searches and review counts.
  2. Track new links by relevance and source, not only quantity.
  3. Watch referral traffic, since a good link also sends visitors.
  4. Monitor branded search growth in Search Console.
  5. Review each quarter and compare with the plan.
MetricSourceTells you
New referring domains (relevant)Link tool, Search Console links reportLink growth quality
Branded search impressionsSearch ConsoleAwareness growth
Referral sessionsAnalyticsWhether links bring real visitors
Review count and ratingReview platformsTrust signal

Seven off-page mistakes to avoid

  1. Buying links. It risks a penalty and short-lived results.
  2. Chasing volume. A hundred irrelevant links do little.
  3. Over-optimised anchors. Exact-match anchors repeated everywhere look manufactured.
  4. Mass-sent outreach. It is ignored, and it can harm your reputation.
  5. Ignoring reviews. Silence on feedback costs trust.
  6. Inconsistent business details. Mismatched names and addresses confuse users and search engines.
  7. Building links to weak pages. Improve the page first.

Frequently asked questions

What is off-page SEO in simple words?

It is the work done away from your own site to build trust, mainly earning links and mentions from other credible websites.

Are backlinks still important?

Yes. Links remain one of the main signals of trust, though relevance and quality matter far more than count.

Do social media signals help SEO?

They are not a confirmed direct ranking factor, but social attention can lead to links, mentions and traffic that do help.

How long does off-page SEO take?

Usually months. Links and reputation accumulate slowly, so plan on a quarter or more before judging.

Is link building safe?

Earning links through useful content and honest outreach is safe. Buying links or running networks to influence rankings breaks search engine policies.

Conclusion

Off-page SEO is the long game of earning trust. Build something worth citing, put it in front of the right people, keep your public details consistent and measure quality, not volume.

title: Technical SEO: How to Make Your Site Easy to Crawl, Index and Load
metaDescription: Technical SEO explained for non-developers: crawling, indexing, site speed, redirects and structured data, with a checklist and a 30-day plan.
excerpt: Technical SEO explained for non-developers: crawling, indexing, site speed, redirects and structured data, with a checklist and a 30-day plan.
coverAlt: Cover: technical SEO guide with a server stack icon
author: Prabal Raj Shakya
body:
Key Takeaways

  • Technical SEO is the gatekeeper. A page must be crawled and indexed before it can compete.
  • Most sites need a handful of fixes, not a rebuild: indexing, redirects, duplicates, speed and mobile.
  • Check with free tools first: Google Search Console, a crawler such as Screaming Frog, and PageSpeed Insights.
  • Speed is part of user experience. Aim for pages that load quickly and stay stable.
  • Re-test after every change, and keep a change log.
From my own work: At GSA Contract Services I run ongoing technical SEO audits with Screaming Frog, and I use Detailed SEO, Wappalyzer and SEO Minion for on-page and tech-stack checks. The audit order below mirrors that routine.

Technical SEO means making sure a search engine can reach, read and store your pages without obstacles: no broken links, slow loading, duplicate pages or a blocked robots.txt. If this layer fails, nothing built on top of it can rank.

This guide explains what to check, how technical SEO differs from on-page and off-page work, what to fix first, and how to confirm the fixes worked.

New to SEO? Start with what SEO is and how it works, then come back here.

What technical SEO covers

Technical SEO answers one question: "Can a search engine reach and read this site?" It breaks into five areas.

AreaWhat to checkCommon problem
Crawlingrobots.txt, internal links, XML sitemapImportant pages blocked or unlinked
IndexingNoindex tags, canonicals, status codesKey pages not in the index; duplicate versions
RenderingWhether content appears without heavy scriptsContent only visible after JavaScript runs
Speed and stabilityCore Web Vitals, image size, server responseSlow pages, layout shifts
Structure and markupURLs, redirects, HTTPS, structured dataRedirect chains, mixed content, wrong schema

Technical SEO vs on-page vs off-page SEO

Technical vs on-page

Technical SEO decides whether a page can be found and processed. On-page SEO decides how well it competes once processed. A beautifully written page that is set to noindex will never rank, and a fast, clean page with vague content will not either.

Technical vs off-page

Off-page work brings trust from other sites. Technical issues can waste that trust: a page with many links that returns an error, or redirects through several steps, loses value on the way.

Fixes vs maintenance

Technical SEO is not a one-time job. Sites change: plugins update, developers release, templates shift. A monthly check catches problems before they cost traffic.

Where technical SEO fits

Technical SEO comes first in the sequence. Make the site accessible, then improve the pages with {{link:on-page-seo|on-page SEO}}, then earn trust with {{link:off-page-seo|off-page SEO}}.

It also matters for ecommerce, where filters and variants can create thousands of duplicate pages. See {{link:ecommerce-seo|ecommerce SEO}}.

What to fix first

Prioritise by how much each problem blocks visibility.

What you findPriorityWhy
Key pages not indexedCriticalNo index, no rankings.
Site or section blocked in robots.txtCriticalSearch engines cannot crawl it.
Wrong canonical or duplicate versions of the siteHighSplits signals between versions.
Broken links and long redirect chainsHighWaste crawl effort and lose link value.
Slow pages, layout shiftsMedium to highHurts users and can hurt rankings.
Missing or wrong structured dataMediumLimits rich results.

How to run a technical SEO audit

Use free or low-cost tools and work in this order.

  1. Check indexing in Search Console. Open the page indexing report and read the reasons pages are excluded.
  2. Test robots.txt. Confirm you are not blocking pages, scripts or styles that matter.
  3. Submit and review the XML sitemap. Only list pages that should be indexed, returning a 200 status.
  4. Crawl the site. Use a crawler to find broken links, redirect chains, duplicate titles, missing canonicals and orphan pages.
  5. Fix duplicates. Choose one version of each page (with or without www, HTTP vs HTTPS) and redirect the rest. Use canonical tags for near-duplicates.
  6. Check mobile usability and rendering. View the page as Google does using the URL inspection tool.
  7. Test speed. Run key templates through PageSpeed Insights. Fix the biggest items first: large images, heavy scripts, slow server response.
  8. Review HTTPS. Valid certificate, no mixed content, all versions redirect to HTTPS.
  9. Add structured data that matches visible content, then validate it.
  10. Log every change with the date so you can link results to causes.

Before and after: a redirect chain.

BeforeAfter
http://example.com/old → https://example.com/old → https://www.example.com/old → https://www.example.com/newhttp://example.com/old → https://www.example.com/new (one step)

Fewer hops mean faster loads and less lost value. Update internal links to point straight at the final URL.

Want a technical SEO audit?

I'll crawl your site, check indexing and speed, and give you a ranked list of fixes.

Request a technical auditSee my SEO expertise

Technical SEO checklist

  • Key pages are indexed and return a 200 status.
  • robots.txt allows what should be crawled, and blocks only what should not be.
  • XML sitemap lists only canonical, indexable pages.
  • One version of the site resolves; the rest redirect in one step.
  • No broken internal links; redirect chains removed.
  • Canonical tags point to the right page.
  • Mobile layout works; main content is visible without heavy scripts.
  • Core Web Vitals in the good range on key templates.
  • HTTPS everywhere, no mixed content.
  • Structured data valid and matching the page.

A 30-day technical plan

WeekFocusOutput
1DiagnoseSearch Console review and a full site crawl. List and rank issues.
2Fix blockersIndexing, robots.txt, canonicals, redirects.
3Speed and mobileImage compression, script clean-up, layout fixes.
4Verify and monitorRe-crawl, validate in Search Console, set a monthly check.

How to measure technical SEO

Technical fixes show up as clean reports first, then as traffic.

  1. Baseline: number of indexed pages, crawl errors, Core Web Vitals status and average load time on key pages.
  2. After fixes, use Search Console’s validate fix option where offered.
  3. Watch indexed pages and the share of pages with errors.
  4. Watch crawl stats for fewer errors and faster response.
  5. Compare traffic to affected pages in the weeks after.
MetricSourceTells you
Indexed pages vs expectedSearch ConsoleWhether key pages are stored
Core Web Vitals pass rateSearch Console, PageSpeed InsightsSpeed and stability
Crawl errorsSearch Console, crawlerRemaining blockers
Organic traffic to fixed pagesAnalyticsBusiness impact

Seven technical SEO mistakes to avoid

  1. Blocking the whole site by accident, often left over from a staging setup.
  2. Noindex left on after launch.
  3. Listing broken or redirected URLs in the sitemap.
  4. Redirect chains and loops.
  5. Ignoring mobile. Most visits come from phones.
  6. Heavy, uncompressed images.
  7. Adding schema for content that is not on the page.

Frequently asked questions

What is technical SEO in simple words?

It is making sure search engines can reach and read your site without problems like broken links, slow loading, duplicate pages or blocked content.

Do I need a developer for technical SEO?

You can find most issues yourself with free tools. Fixing some of them, such as server speed and code changes, usually needs a developer.

How often should I run a technical audit?

A light check monthly and a full audit every quarter or after major site changes.

Does site speed affect rankings?

Page experience is one of many signals, and speed clearly affects how users behave. Fix the biggest slowdowns first.

What is the first thing to check?

Whether your important pages are indexed. Use Search Console to confirm.

Conclusion

Technical SEO is the base your other work stands on. Check indexing first, clean up duplicates and redirects, speed up key pages and keep a monthly routine so problems never build up.

If you would like an expert audit, get in touch and I will review crawling, indexing and speed on your site.

Ready to put this into practice?

title: Local SEO: How to Rank for "Near Me" Searches in Kathmandu and Beyond
metaTitle: Local SEO in Nepal: Rank on Maps
metaDescription: Local SEO explained for Nepali businesses: Google Business Profile, reviews, listings and local pages, with a checklist and a 60-day plan.
excerpt: Local SEO explained for Nepali businesses: Google Business Profile, reviews, listings and local pages, with a checklist and a 60-day plan.
coverAlt: Cover: local SEO guide with a map pin icon
author: Prabal Raj Shakya
body:
Key Takeaways

  • Google uses three main ideas to rank local results: relevance, distance and prominence.
  • Your Google Business Profile is the main asset. Complete it and keep it current.
  • Reviews and consistent details build trust. Answer every review.
  • You need local pages on your site for each service and area you serve.
  • Results are measured in calls, directions and visits, not only clicks.
From my own work: I use GMB Everywhere alongside my other tools to check on-page, local and technical SEO at GSA Contract Services, and I am based in Kathmandu, so the examples come from a market I know.

Local SEO targets searches tied to a place, like "plumber in Kathmandu," and depends heavily on a complete Google Business Profile and consistent listings. It decides who appears in the map results at the top of the page.

This guide explains how local SEO works, how it differs from regular SEO, what to set up first and how to track results, with examples for Nepali businesses.

New to SEO? Start with what SEO is and how it works, then come back here.

How local SEO works

Local search results usually show a map with three listings, then regular results. Google chooses which businesses to show using three ideas.

FactorWhat it meansWhat you can do
RelevanceHow well your listing matches the searchChoose the right categories, describe services, add products
DistanceHow far you are from the searcher or the place namedKeep your address accurate. You cannot change distance, only your listing quality
ProminenceHow well known and trusted you areEarn reviews, citations, links and mentions

Local SEO vs regular SEO vs ecommerce SEO

Local vs regular SEO

Regular SEO competes for a ranked list of pages. Local SEO competes for a place in the map results and for location-based queries. It relies more on your Business Profile, reviews and listing consistency than on blog content.

Local vs ecommerce SEO

Ecommerce SEO helps products rank wherever the buyer lives. Local SEO helps a physical business be found by people nearby. A shop with both a store and an online shop needs both.

Profile work vs website work

The Business Profile earns the map listing. The website earns the trust behind it and ranks in normal results. Neglect either and you lose half the opportunity.

Where local SEO fits

Local SEO sits on top of a sound site. Make sure your site is fast and mobile friendly with good {{link:technical-seo|technical SEO}}, and that your service pages follow {{link:on-page-seo|on-page SEO}} basics.

Reviews, citations and local links are part of {{link:off-page-seo|off-page SEO}}.

What to do first

Pick based on where you are today.

Your situationDo firstWhy
No Business ProfileCreate and verify oneIt is the base of local visibility.
Profile exists but is incompleteFill every field, add photosCompleteness helps relevance and conversions.
Few reviewsStart a review routineProminence and trust.
One location, several servicesBuild a page per serviceMatches more searches.
Several locationsA profile and a page per locationEach place needs its own listing.

How to do local SEO, step by step

Follow the order below.

  1. Claim and verify your Google Business Profile.
  2. Choose the right primary category and add relevant secondary ones.
  3. Complete every field: name, address, phone, hours, services, description, website, and a short, honest description of what you do.
  4. Add real photos of the shop, team and work. Update them regularly.
  5. Keep your name, address and phone the same everywhere. Check your website, social profiles and directories.
  6. Ask happy customers for reviews and reply to all of them politely, including the bad ones.
  7. Build a page for each service and area with real details: what you offer, where, prices or ranges, and photos.
  8. Embed a map and add LocalBusiness structured data that matches the visible details.
  9. List your business in relevant directories and local sites. Quality over quantity.
  10. Post updates on the profile such as offers and events.

Before and after: a service page opening.

BeforeAfter
"We offer plumbing services at affordable prices. Contact us.""We repair leaks and install water tanks across Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur. Call before 4 pm for a same-day visit. Open Sunday to Friday."

The second version names the services, the areas and the hours. Replace these with your real details.

Want more calls from Google Maps?

I'll review your Business Profile, listings and local pages and show you what to fix first.

Request a local SEO reviewSee my SEO expertise

Local SEO checklist

  • Business Profile verified and complete.
  • Correct categories and services listed.
  • Name, address and phone identical on every platform.
  • New reviews arriving monthly and answered.
  • A page for each service and area.
  • LocalBusiness schema on the site.
  • Listings in relevant directories.
  • Mobile site loads quickly with a click-to-call button.

A 60-day local plan

WeeksFocusOutput
1 to 2Profile and consistencyVerify, complete the profile, fix all name and address mismatches.
3 to 4Site pagesPublish service and area pages. Add schema and a map.
5 to 6Reviews and listingsStart the review routine. Submit to relevant directories.
7 to 8Measure and adjustRecord calls, direction requests and website clicks. Compare with the baseline.

How to measure local SEO

Local success shows in actions, not only visits.

  1. Baseline: calls, direction requests and website clicks from the Business Profile insights.
  2. Track review count, rating and response rate.
  3. Check local rankings from a few spots in your service area, using incognito or a tracking tool.
  4. Count enquiries that mention they found you on Google.
  5. Review monthly.
MetricSourceTells you
Calls and direction requestsBusiness Profile insightsReal-world demand
Reviews and ratingBusiness ProfileTrust and prominence
Local ranking by areaManual check or toolVisibility on the map
Website clicks from local queriesSearch ConsoleSite performance

Seven local SEO mistakes to avoid

  1. Keyword stuffing the business name. Use your real name.
  2. Inconsistent name, address or phone.
  3. Ignoring reviews, especially negative ones.
  4. Fake or bought reviews. They risk removal and loss of trust.
  5. One generic page for every service and area.
  6. Wrong or too many categories.
  7. Letting hours and details go out of date.

Frequently asked questions

What is local SEO in simple words?

It is helping your business show up when people search for something near them, such as "dentist in Lalitpur", especially in the map results.

Do I need a website for local SEO?

A Business Profile can bring visibility on its own, but a website builds trust and helps you rank in regular results.

How do I get more Google reviews?

Ask real customers soon after a good experience, make it easy with a direct link, and reply to every review.

How long does local SEO take?

Profile improvements can show within weeks. Building reviews and prominence takes months.

Can I rank in several cities?

You can rank in places where you have a real presence or serve customers. Create pages for areas you genuinely serve, not empty pages for every town.

Conclusion

Local SEO is practical and measurable. Get your profile verified and complete, keep your details consistent, earn honest reviews and build pages for the services and areas you actually cover.

If you want a local audit for your business, get in touch and I will review your profile and site.

Ready to put this into practice?

Tell me about your site and your goals. I will reply within a day with where I would start.

title: Ecommerce SEO: Product Pages, Category Pages and Filters That Actually Rank
metaTitle: Ecommerce SEO: Product and Category Pages
metaDescription: Ecommerce SEO explained: product pages, category structure, duplicate filter pages, schema and reviews, with a checklist and a 60-day plan.
excerpt: Ecommerce SEO explained: product pages, category structure, duplicate filter pages, schema and reviews, with a checklist and a 60-day plan.
coverAlt: Cover: ecommerce SEO guide with a shopping bag icon
author: Prabal Raj Shakya
body:
Key Takeaways

  • Category pages usually carry the most search demand. People search "running shoes" before they search one model.
  • Each product page needs unique content, not the manufacturer’s copy pasted across the web.
  • Filters and variants can create thousands of duplicate pages. Control them with canonicals and crawl rules.
  • Structured data helps search engines read price, stock and reviews.
  • Measure revenue, not only traffic.
How this guide was made: My day-to-day work is technical SEO audits and on-page optimisation. For online stores I lean on Google's published guidance on product pages and duplicate URLs, linked in the sources below, and I flag the parts that depend on your platform.

Ecommerce SEO applies the same ideas as regular SEO to online stores, with extra attention to product pages, category structure and the duplicate content that filters create. Its goal is simple: put the right product in front of someone who is ready to buy.

This guide explains where store SEO differs from regular SEO, which pages to fix first, how to handle filters and variants, and how to measure revenue impact.

New to SEO? Start with what SEO is and how it works, then come back here.

What makes ecommerce SEO different

A store has far more pages than most sites, many near-identical, and its searchers are closer to buying. That changes where the effort goes.

Page typeSearcher intentMain SEO job
Home pageBrand or general browsingClear navigation, links to top categories
Category pageExploring a type of productRank for the broad term, show useful filters and copy
Product pageReady to buy a specific itemUnique description, reviews, schema, clear price and stock
Blog or guideResearching before buyingAnswer questions and link to products
Filtered or sorted URLsRefining a listUsually kept out of the index to avoid duplicates

Ecommerce SEO vs regular SEO vs local SEO

Ecommerce vs regular SEO

A content site publishes a few hundred pages and each one matters. A store may publish thousands of product pages that are close variations. The challenge shifts from writing everything to managing scale: structure, duplication and templates.

Ecommerce vs local SEO

Local SEO helps a physical business appear for nearby searches. Ecommerce SEO serves buyers anywhere you ship. A shop with a store and a web shop needs both. See {{link:local-seo|local SEO}} for the store side.

Product pages vs category pages

Category pages target broad searches and usually have the largest audience. Product pages catch buyers with specific intent. A store that optimises only products misses the bigger demand.

Where ecommerce SEO fits

Stores depend on {{link:technical-seo|technical SEO}} more than most sites because of scale: crawl budget, duplicate URLs and page speed matter. Product copy follows {{link:on-page-seo|on-page SEO}} principles, and reviews and mentions feed {{link:off-page-seo|off-page SEO}}.

What to fix first

Match the fix to the symptom.

What you seeDo firstWhy
Thousands of filter URLs in the indexCanonical and noindex rules, tidy internal linksStops duplicate pages competing.
Product pages with manufacturer copyWrite unique descriptions for best sellersOriginal content stands out.
Thin category pagesAdd helpful intro text and clear subcategoriesThese pages target the biggest demand.
Slow product pagesCompress images, reduce scriptsSpeed affects conversion as well as SEO.
No reviewsStart collecting themTrust, and review content for rich results.

How to do ecommerce SEO, step by step

Work from structure down to detail.

  1. Plan the site structure. A shallow tree: home, categories, subcategories, products. Keep important products within a few clicks of the home page.
  2. Research keywords by page type. Broad terms for categories, specific terms and model names for products.
  3. Optimise category pages. A clear H1, a short helpful intro, visible subcategories and links to best sellers. Put long text below the products if it hurts usability.
  4. Write unique product pages. Describe use, size, materials, who it suits and what makes it different. Add specifications and honest photos.
  5. Handle filters and variants. Use canonical tags to the main version, keep parameter pages out of the index and avoid linking to every combination.
  6. Add Product structured data with name, image, price, availability and reviews that match what the page shows.
  7. Show real reviews and Q&A on product pages.
  8. Use breadcrumbs and internal links so crawlers and shoppers can move through the store.
  9. Deal with out-of-stock and discontinued items. Keep pages for items that return, redirect permanently removed items to the closest alternative.
  10. Improve speed on mobile. Compress images, lazy-load below the fold, limit third-party scripts.

Before and after: a product description.

BeforeAfter
"Premium quality backpack. Durable and stylish. Buy now.""A 25-litre daily backpack in water-resistant nylon with a padded laptop sleeve (fits up to 15 inches) and a hidden back pocket. Weighs 780 g. Comes in black, olive and navy."

The second version gives facts a buyer can compare. Use your real specifications.

Want your online store audited?

I'll check your structure, duplicate pages and product content and show you where the sales are being lost.

Request a store auditSee my SEO expertise

Ecommerce SEO checklist

  • Clear category tree with descriptive names.
  • Category pages with a clear H1 and useful intro.
  • Unique product titles and descriptions.
  • Filter and sort pages controlled with canonicals or noindex.
  • Product structured data valid and matching the page.
  • Reviews visible and genuine.
  • Breadcrumbs on every product and category page.
  • Stock and price accurate and consistent.
  • Mobile speed in the good range.
  • Sitemap lists canonical product and category URLs only.

A 60-day ecommerce plan

WeeksFocusOutput
1 to 2AuditCrawl the store. Count indexed pages vs real pages. List duplicate and thin page groups.
3 to 4Structure and duplicatesFix filters, canonicals, redirects, sitemap.
5 to 6Category and product contentRewrite top categories and best-selling products.
7 to 8Schema, reviews, measureAdd structured data, start review collection, compare against baseline.

How to measure ecommerce SEO

Tie SEO to sales.

  1. Baseline: organic sessions, organic revenue, conversion rate and indexed pages.
  2. Track by page type: category, product, blog.
  3. Check Search Console for impressions and clicks on category queries.
  4. Compare revenue per organic session before and after changes.
  5. Review monthly, and expect category improvements to take a few months.
MetricSourceTells you
Organic revenue and conversion rateAnalyticsBusiness impact
Clicks on category queriesSearch ConsoleVisibility for broad demand
Indexed vs total pagesSearch ConsoleDuplicate and thin page control
Product page speedPageSpeed InsightsUser experience

Seven ecommerce SEO mistakes to avoid

  1. Copying manufacturer descriptions.
  2. Letting filters create endless indexed URLs.
  3. Ignoring category pages.
  4. Deleting out-of-stock pages without a plan.
  5. Fake or incentivised-without-disclosure reviews.
  6. Wrong price or availability in structured data.
  7. Slow mobile pages with heavy images.

Frequently asked questions

What is ecommerce SEO in simple words?

It is helping the pages of an online store show up on search engines so shoppers can find the right products.

Which pages matter most?

Category pages usually have the largest search demand. Product pages capture buyers with specific intent. Both matter.

How do I stop duplicate content from filters?

Use canonical tags pointing to the main version, keep parameter pages out of the index and avoid linking to every filter combination.

What should I do with out-of-stock products?

Keep the page if the item will return and say so. If it is gone for good, redirect to the closest alternative.

How long does ecommerce SEO take?

Technical fixes can help within weeks. Category rankings and revenue usually take a few months.

Conclusion

Ecommerce SEO rewards structure and discipline. Build clear categories, write product pages that help a buyer decide, control the duplicate URLs filters create and tie your measurement to revenue.

If you would like an audit of your store, get in touch and I will review structure, duplicates and product pages.

Ready to put this into practice?

Tell me about your site and your goals. I will reply within a day with where I would start.

faq.q: What is ecommerce SEO in simple words?
faq.a: It is helping the pages of an online store show up on search engines so shoppers can find the right products.

faq.q: Which pages matter most?
faq.a: Category pages usually have the largest search demand. Product pages capture buyers with specific intent. Both matter.

faq.q: How do I stop duplicate content from filters?
faq.a: Use canonical tags pointing to the main version, keep parameter pages out of the index and avoid linking to every filter combination.

faq.q: What should I do with out-of-stock products?
faq.a: Keep the page if the item will return and say so. If it is gone for good, redirect to the closest alternative.

faq.q: How long does ecommerce SEO take?
faq.a: Technical fixes can help within weeks. Category rankings and revenue usually take a few months.

title: YouTube SEO: How to Rank Videos and Get Recommended
metaTitle: YouTube SEO: Rank and Get Suggested
metaDescription: YouTube SEO explained: titles, descriptions, captions, thumbnails and chapters, how it differs from Google SEO, with a checklist and a 30-day plan.
excerpt: YouTube SEO explained: titles, descriptions, captions, thumbnails and chapters, how it differs from Google SEO, with a checklist and a 30-day plan.
coverAlt: Cover: YouTube SEO guide with a video player icon
author: Prabal Raj Shakya
body:
Key Takeaways

  • YouTube has two doors: search (people looking) and recommendations (browse, suggested, home).
  • Titles and thumbnails earn the click; the video earns the watch time.
  • Description, captions and chapters tell YouTube what the video is about.
  • Viewer satisfaction is the main signal. Keep people watching and coming back.
  • Check performance by video and by traffic source in YouTube Studio.
From my own work: I edit short talking-head videos in CapCut and have training in video editing, so the advice on openings, pacing and thumbnails comes from editing, backed by YouTube's own help pages and Google's video guidance.

YouTube SEO means giving your videos accurate titles, descriptions, captions and thumbnails that help YouTube’s own search and recommendation system understand them, and giving viewers a reason to keep watching. It also helps videos appear in Google results.

This guide explains how YouTube ranks videos, how it differs from website SEO, what to set up on every upload and how to measure what is working.

New to SEO? Start with what SEO is and how it works, then come back here.

How YouTube SEO works

YouTube’s system tries to show each viewer videos they will watch and enjoy. Several pieces feed that decision.

ElementWhat it doesWhat to do
TitleTells people and YouTube what the video isLead with the main phrase, be specific
ThumbnailEarns the clickClear subject, readable text, consistent style
DescriptionGives context and keywordsPut the key information in the first lines, add links and timestamps
CaptionsMake the video accessible and searchableUpload or correct subtitles
ChaptersHelp viewers jump and help YouTube understandAdd timestamps with clear names
Watch time and engagementShows whether viewers like the videoOpen with the point, keep pace, deliver on the title

YouTube SEO vs Google SEO vs social media

YouTube SEO vs website SEO

Website SEO competes on pages and links. YouTube SEO competes on viewer behaviour: clicks, watch time and return visits. Metadata matters, but a video that holds attention can outperform a perfectly labelled one that does not.

Search vs recommendations

Search traffic comes from people typing a question. Recommended traffic comes from YouTube suggesting your video to people watching similar content. Strong titles help the first, strong retention helps the second.

YouTube vs Google results

Videos can also appear in Google search. A clear title, a good description and a page on your site that embeds the video help it be found in both places.

Where YouTube SEO fits

Video supports the rest of your marketing. Embed videos on pages you have optimised with {{link:on-page-seo|on-page SEO}}, and link your channel from your site to help {{link:off-page-seo|off-page SEO}} signals. Local businesses can add video to their profiles. See {{link:local-seo|local SEO}}.

What to do first

Choose by your channel’s stage.

Your situationDo firstWhy
New channelPick one topic and make five videos around itHelps YouTube learn who to show you to.
Views but low clicksImprove titles and thumbnailsPeople see you but do not click.
Clicks but people leave quicklyFix openings and pacingRetention drives recommendations.
Good videos, few searchesImprove descriptions, captions and chaptersBetter context for search.
Old libraryRefresh titles and thumbnails on top videosQuick gains from existing content.

How to optimise a YouTube video, step by step

Follow this for every upload.

  1. Research the topic. Use YouTube search suggestions, comments and your own audience questions.
  2. Write the title for people first. Put the main phrase near the start, keep it honest and specific.
  3. Design the thumbnail. One clear subject, a few big words at most, high contrast, a consistent look.
  4. Open with the point. Say what the viewer will get in the first moments and deliver it.
  5. Write a useful description. The first lines should summarise the video. Add links, resources and timestamps.
  6. Add chapters with clear names.
  7. Upload accurate captions and a transcript. Correct auto-generated mistakes.
  8. Choose a category and relevant tags sparingly. Tags matter little. Do not stuff them.
  9. Add cards and end screens pointing to the next video, and build playlists.
  10. Embed the video on a relevant page of your site and share it where your audience is.

Before and after: a title and description opening.

BeforeAfter
Title: "Marketing tips 2026!!!"
Description: "Subscribe and like. Please follow us."		Title: "How to Get Your First 100 Customers With Facebook Ads (Step by Step)"
Description: "In this video: how to set a budget, pick an audience and test three ads. 0:00 Intro, 1:10 Budget, 3:40 Audience."

The second version states the promise, the topic and the structure. Use your own real content.

Planning a video strategy?

I'll help you map topics, titles and thumbnails so the right viewers find your videos.

Plan my video strategySee my SEO expertise

YouTube SEO checklist

  • One topic and one promise per video.
  • Title: main phrase first, specific, honest.
  • Thumbnail clear and consistent.
  • Strong opening that confirms what the video delivers.
  • Description: summary first, links and timestamps.
  • Chapters added.
  • Captions corrected.
  • Cards, end screen and playlist set.
  • Video embedded on a relevant page.

A 30-day YouTube plan

WeekFocusOutput
1ResearchList 15 questions your audience asks. Review top competitors’ titles and thumbnails.
2Refresh the libraryUpdate titles, thumbnails, descriptions and chapters on your five best videos.
3PublishRelease two optimised videos on one topic cluster.
4ReviewCompare click-through rate, retention and traffic sources in YouTube Studio.

How to measure YouTube SEO

YouTube Studio shows most of what you need.

  1. Baseline: impressions, click-through rate, average view duration and traffic sources for your top videos.
  2. Compare before and after each title or thumbnail change, over the same length of time.
  3. Check traffic sources: YouTube search, suggested, browse and external.
  4. Look at retention graphs to see where viewers leave.
  5. Review monthly.
MetricSourceTells you
Impressions click-through rateYouTube StudioWhether title and thumbnail work
Average view duration and retentionYouTube StudioWhether the video holds attention
Traffic by sourceYouTube StudioSearch vs recommended reach
Subscribers gained per videoYouTube StudioWhether viewers want more

Seven YouTube SEO mistakes to avoid

  1. Misleading titles or thumbnails. Viewers leave and trust drops.
  2. Stuffing tags and descriptions with keywords.
  3. Slow openings.
  4. No captions.
  5. Ignoring analytics.
  6. Random topics. A focused channel is easier for YouTube to place.
  7. Never refreshing old videos.

Frequently asked questions

What is YouTube SEO in simple words?

It is setting up your videos so YouTube understands them and viewers want to watch them, which helps them appear in search and recommendations.

Do tags still matter?

Very little. Titles, thumbnails, descriptions and viewer behaviour matter far more. Add a few relevant tags and move on.

How long should my video be?

As long as it takes to deliver what the title promises. Retention matters more than length.

Do captions help rankings?

They help accessibility and give YouTube more text to understand, so they are worth adding.

How long does YouTube SEO take?

Updates to metadata can help within weeks. Growing a channel takes months of steady uploads.

Conclusion

YouTube rewards videos that people click and keep watching. Write clear titles, design honest thumbnails, open with the point, add captions and chapters and check YouTube Studio each month to keep what works.
